argument: John Rawls set out to defend liberal democracy against its long history of failure by arguing that societies have never had a genuine conversation about what justice, specifically 'distributive justice,' actually requires. Using the veil-of-ignorance thought experiment, he argued rational people designing a society without knowing their place in it would choose the structure that gives the best possible outcome to the worst-off (the 'maximin' rule), and that inequalities are only just when they arise from positions open to all and their benefits flow to the least advantaged, since so much of what makes people unequal is simply morally arbitrary luck.
keyIdeas: Rawls thinks liberal democracy's history of failure stems not from a flaw in the system itself but from never having a substantive conversation about what justice actually requires.
'Primary social goods' are the surplus value produced by cooperating in society, including not just income and wealth but also less obvious goods like rights, liberties, and opportunities.
Much of what makes people unequal, talent, family, luck, even accidents, is 'morally arbitrary': not something a person fully owns or deserves, whether the luck is good or bad.

The veil of ignorance asks people to design a society without knowing their own place within it, so self-interest can't bias the structure they choose; rational people would then follow the 'maximin' rule, picking the society whose worst-case outcome is the best available.

An inequality is just only when it arises from a position open to all (equality of opportunity) and its benefits flow to the least advantaged (the difference principle), not simply from legally possessing wealth.

terms.def: The question of how the surplus value created by social cooperation should be allocated.
The full set of benefits produced by society, including income and wealth but also rights, liberties, and opportunities.
Rawls's thought experiment in which people design a society's structure without knowing their own place within it.
The principle of choosing the social structure whose worst-case outcome for the least advantaged is the best among all options.
The idea that inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged members of society.
